scenes.title: What is Cloud Computing?
scenes.narration: Cloud computing means renting computing resources like servers, storage, and databases over the internet instead of buying and running your own hardware.

scenes.title: Why It Changed Everything
bullets: You pay only for what you use, turning huge upfront hardware costs into flexible operating expenses.
You can provision servers in minutes instead of waiting weeks for physical machines to arrive.
The provider handles the data centers, power, and cooling, so your team focuses on building data products.
scenes.narration: Pay-as-you-go pricing replaces the old model of buying expensive servers you might barely use. Because resources spin up in minutes, teams can experiment quickly and scale on demand. And since the provider owns the physical infrastructure, engineers spend their energy on pipelines and analytics rather than racking hardware.

scenes.title: Cloud Service Models
scenes.narration: The cloud is layered by how much the provider manages for you. Infrastructure as a Service hands you raw building blocks like virtual machines. Platform as a Service manages the runtime so you deploy code, while Software as a Service delivers finished applications you simply log into.

scenes.title: On-Premises vs. Cloud
scenes.narration: With on-premises infrastructure you commit to fixed capacity and shoulder all maintenance yourself. The cloud flips this to elastic, on-demand resources where the provider handles the underlying upkeep. For data workloads that spike and dip, that elasticity is often the deciding factor.

scenes.text: The cloud is someone else's computers rented on demand — you trade upfront ownership for speed, elasticity, and pay-per-use flexibility.
scenes.narration: At its core, the cloud lets you rent infrastructure instead of owning it. That shift buys you speed and elasticity, which is why nearly all modern data platforms are built there.
